newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan makes little headway against oil slick.
newsitem.headline: Japan makes little headway against oil slick.

text.p: Japanese maritime authorities made little headway on Monday in their bid to break up a major oil spill from a sunken Russian tanker that threatens rich fishing grounds off Japan's main island of Honshu.
A Maritime Safety Agency (MSA) spokesman also said there were worries that the spill, already described as the nation's second-biggest, may be worse than expected.
More than a dozen clean-up ships as well as helicopters are involved in efforts to stop the oil reaching the coast.
"We are not sure of the volume of the leaked oil. So far we have relied on the accounts of the tanker crew but we really don't know," the spokesman told Reuters.
"The sunken stern section of the tanker has yet to be found. It's possible oil may be leaking out of it," he added.
A section comprising about two-thirds of the stricken tanker, including the stern, contains the majority of the ship's 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of heavy fuel oil.
The bow section was spotted at about 45 km (28 miles) off central Japan's Fukui prefecture on Monday morning, an MSA official said.

It had earlier been estimated that only 3,700 tonnes (26,000 barrels) of oil had escaped from ruptured tanks in the ship's bow when the 13,157-tonne Nakhodka was torn in two in stormy seas in the Sea of Japan last Thursday.
Japan's biggest oil spill was in 1971, when 7,200 tonnes (50,400 barrels) of oil spilled from a tanker that ran aground near the port city of Niigata.
The spokesman said attempts to disperse two major groups of oil slicks, floating about 52 km (30 miles) off the coasts of Fukui and Ishikawa prefectures, had so far had little success.
The slicks extend about 10 km (five miles) from where the ship sank and are being driven towards shore by strong winds.
"We've tried putting detergent on the slicks and churning them up with the propellers of our boats but as yet we've had no great success," the spokesman said.
The Russian-registered Nakhodka was built 26 years ago and authorities said the age of the ship, which was heading to Russia from China, was probably a factor in it breaking apart in the rough seas.
The 31 crew from the tanker were rescued but the captain was still missing. Officials said there was almost no hope that he had survived.
With winds of up to 50 km per hour (30 miles per hour), MSA officials fear the oil could reach the coast by Wednesday if it is not broken up.
They have alerted producers of shellfish, seaweed and other sea products along the coast about the possibility of extensive environmental damage if the slicks reach the shore.
The agency said the spill had caused no serious disturbance to shipping in the area.
